examples.en: Please write your residential address on the form.
This neighborhood is popular as a place to live.
You have to report it when your residence changes.

examples.ko: 저는 회사와 가까운 곳으로 거주지를 옮겼어요.
examples.en: I moved my residence to a place near the company.
Most students' residences are near the school.
Near the park is quiet, so it's good for living.

explain: '거주지'는 사람이 실제로 사는 곳이에요. 일상에서는 '사는 곳'이나 '집'이라고 하고, 서류에서는 '거주지'나 '주소'라고 써요. 회사 위치는 '소재지'라서 사람과 기관에 쓰는 말이 달라요.
explain_en: 거주지 is where a person actually lives. In daily talk people say 사는 곳 or 집, while forms use 거주지 or 주소. A company's location is 소재지, so the word differs for people and for institutions.

examples.en: My coworker dumped his work on me.

examples.ko: 귀찮은 일을 신입에게 떠맡기면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You shouldn't foist annoying work onto the newcomer.
She left the child with Grandmother and went out.
Why are you pushing all the responsibility onto me?
The team leader suddenly handed the presentation off to me.

examples.ko: 남에게 떠맡기듯이 일하지 말고 직접 해 보세요.
examples.en: Don't work as if you're dumping things on others; try doing it yourself.

explain: 하기 싫거나 부담스러운 일·책임을 억지로 남에게 넘길 때 써요. 받는 쪽에서 말하면 '떠맡다'가 되니까 짝으로 외워 두세요. 대개 불만이나 비판의 느낌이 들어 있어요.
explain_en: Use it when you force an unwanted job or responsibility onto someone else. From the receiver's side the word becomes '떠맡다', so learn them as a pair. It usually carries a feeling of complaint or criticism.

examples.en: The referee gave the player a red card.
A player who gets a red card is sent off right away.
A red card came out for a rough foul.
Two yellow cards are the same as a red card.
We lost today's match because of a red card.
That player was sent off with a red card.

explain: 축구 같은 경기에서 반칙을 크게 했을 때 심판이 꺼내는 카드로, 받으면 퇴장해요. 가벼운 경고는 '옐로카드'라고 해요. 보통 '레드카드를 받다', '레드카드를 꺼내다'로 말해요.
explain_en: In sports like soccer, this is the card a referee shows for a serious foul, and the player must leave. A lighter warning is a '옐로카드'. It is usually said as '레드카드를 받다' or '레드카드를 꺼내다'.

en: to lodge temporarily; to stay at someone's home

examples.en: On Jeju Island I stayed at a small private guesthouse.
This summer I will stay at a seaside guesthouse.

examples.ko: 호텔보다 시골집에 민박하는 게 더 좋아요.
examples.en: I like staying at a country house better than a hotel.
After hiking, we stayed overnight at a village guesthouse.
The landlady gave breakfast to the guests staying overnight.

examples.ko: 예약 없이 민박하려고 했는데 방이 없었어요.
examples.en: I tried to stay without a reservation, but there was no room.

explain: 일반 가정집이나 작은 집에서 돈을 내고 하룻밤 자는 것을 말해요. 호텔이나 모텔 같은 숙박업소와 다르게 주인이 사는 집인 경우가 많아요. '펜션'은 가족 단위로 빌리는 별장 느낌이라 달라요.
explain_en: It means paying to sleep a night in an ordinary home or small house. Unlike a hotel or motel, the owner often lives there. A 펜션 feels like a rented villa for families, which is different.

examples.en: My grandmother wove a basket out of wheat straw.
In summer, I go out to the field wearing a straw hat.

examples.ko: 밀짚 가방은 여름 바다에 잘 어울려요.
examples.en: A straw bag goes well with the summer sea.

examples.ko: 마당에 밀짚을 깔고 말린 고추를 널었어요.
examples.en: We spread straw in the yard and laid out the dried peppers.

examples.ko: 밀짚 냄새를 맡으니 어릴 때 시골이 생각났어요.
examples.en: The smell of straw reminded me of the countryside from my childhood.

examples.ko: 시골 체험에서 밀짚 인형을 만들어 봤어요.
examples.en: At the countryside experience program, I made a straw doll.

explain: 밀을 거두고 남은 줄기를 말려 만든 것이에요. 일상에서는 '밀짚모자'로 가장 많이 만나요. 음료를 마시는 '빨대'와 헷갈리지 마세요.
explain_en: It is the dried stalk left after wheat is harvested. In daily life you most often meet it in '밀짚모자' (straw hat). Don't confuse it with '빨대', the drinking straw.

en: with a scratching sound; with scrape

examples.en: My arm was itchy, so I scratched it hard.

examples.ko: 빨래에 묻은 얼룩을 벅벅 문질러 닦았어요.
examples.en: I scrubbed the stain on the laundry hard to clean it.

examples.ko: 개가 문을 벅벅 긁는 소리가 들려요.
examples.en: I can hear the dog scratching at the door.
The child scrubbed his hair vigorously and came out.
I'm upset because the cat keeps scratching the sofa.

examples.ko: 그는 졸린 얼굴을 손으로 벅벅 비볐어요.
examples.en: He rubbed his sleepy face hard with his hands.

explain: 거칠고 힘주어 긁거나 문지를 때 쓰는 말이에요. '박박'과 비슷하지만 소리가 더 굵게 들려요. 보통 '벅벅 긁다', '벅벅 문지르다'처럼 써요.
explain_en: It is used for scratching or rubbing roughly and with force. It is similar to '박박' but sounds deeper and heavier. It usually appears as '벅벅 긁다' or '벅벅 문지르다'.

examples.ko: 물이 빠진 갯벌에서 비릿한 냄새가 풍겨 왔어요.
examples.en: A slightly fishy smell drifted from the mudflat after the water went out.

examples.ko: 시장 생선 가게 앞은 비릿해서 코를 막았어요.
examples.en: The area in front of the fish shop at the market was fishy, so I covered my nose.
I touched fish and my hands still smell a bit fishy.
The clams may not have been fresh; my mouth tasted fishy.
If it tastes fishy, try squeezing some lemon on it.

examples.ko: 생선이 오래돼서 냄새가 비릿하지 않나 확인했어요.
examples.en: The fish was old, so I checked whether it smelled fishy.

explain: 생선, 피, 갯벌 같은 데서 나는 날 냄새를 말해요. '비린내'가 명사이고 '비릿하다'는 약간 비린 듯하다는 느낌이에요. 냄새뿐 아니라 입안의 맛에도 쓸 수 있어요.
explain_en: It describes the raw smell that comes from fish, blood, or mudflats. '비린내' is the noun, and '비릿하다' means slightly fishy. It can describe taste in the mouth as well as smell.

en: saju; four pillars of destiny; fate

examples.en: I went to a fortune teller to have my sajupalja read.
They said I have a lot of water in my sajupalja.

examples.ko: 사주팔자는 태어난 해, 달, 날, 시간으로 본대요.
examples.en: I heard sajupalja is read from the year, month, day and hour of birth.

examples.ko: 사주팔자를 믿는 사람도 있고 안 믿는 사람도 있어요.
examples.en: Some people believe in sajupalja and some don't.

examples.ko: 사주팔자 탓하지 말고 직접 노력해 보세요.
examples.en: Don't blame your fate; try working at it yourself.

examples.ko: 친구가 사주팔자를 봐 줬는데 신기하게 잘 맞았어요.
examples.en: My friend read my sajupalja, and it was strangely accurate.

explain: 태어난 연, 월, 일, 시로 운명을 보는 전통적인 방법을 말하고, 타고난 운명이라는 뜻으로 넓게 쓰기도 해요. '사주를 보다', '사주팔자를 믿다'처럼 말하고, 줄여서 그냥 '사주'라고도 자주 해요. 대화에서는 '팔자'만 따로 써서 인생의 운을 말하기도 해요.
explain_en: It refers to the traditional way of reading fate from the year, month, day and hour of birth, and is also used loosely for one's destiny. People say '사주를 보다' or '사주팔자를 믿다', and often shorten it to '사주'. In conversation, '팔자' alone is also used to talk about one's life luck.

examples.en: The library shelves are full of books.

examples.ko: 저는 서가 사이를 걸으며 읽을 책을 골랐어요.
examples.en: I walked between the shelves and picked a book to read.
I finally found the book I was looking for on the shelf.
My father's bookshelf has many old books.
I put the newly arrived books on the shelf.

examples.ko: 서가 맨 위 칸은 손이 안 닿아요.
examples.en: I can't reach the top shelf.

explain: 집에서 쓰는 가구는 '책장'이나 '책꽂이'라고 하고, '서가'는 도서관·서점·서재처럼 책이 많은 곳의 책꽂이를 말할 때 어울려요. '책꽂이'는 작은 것, '책장'은 큰 가구에 가까워요. 도서관에서 '서가 번호'를 보고 책을 찾아요.
explain_en: At home people say 책장 or 책꽂이; 서가 suits libraries, bookstores and studies with many books. 책꽂이 leans small, 책장 leans toward a larger piece of furniture. In a library you find books by the 서가 number.

en: to preach; to give a sermon; to lecture (moralizing)

examples.en: The pastor preaches every Sunday.

examples.ko: 아버지가 또 인생에 대해 설교하기 시작했어요.
examples.en: My father started lecturing me about life again.
Don't lecture me.

examples.ko: 선배가 설교하는 말투로 말해서 듣기 싫었어요.
examples.en: The senior spoke in a preachy tone and I didn't want to listen.
At the church, the priest preached about forgiveness.

examples.ko: 친구는 내 잘못을 설교해서 기분이 상했어요.
examples.en: My friend lectured me about my mistake and I felt hurt.

explain: 설교하다는 원래 교회에서 종교 이야기를 전하는 일이에요. 일상에서는 윗사람이 길게 훈계하듯 말할 때 '설교하지 마'처럼 부정적으로 써요. '잔소리하다'는 짧게 반복되는 말, 설교하다는 길고 도덕적인 말이라는 점이 달라요.
explain_en: 설교하다 originally refers to delivering a religious message at church. In daily life it is used negatively, as in 설교하지 마 ('don't preach at me'), when someone talks down at length. 잔소리하다 is short and repeated nagging, while 설교하다 is long and moralizing.

en: warmest part of an ondol floor

examples.en: In winter, the warmest part of the floor is the best.
Grandmother spread the blanket on the warm part of the floor.
I sat on the warm spot of the floor and ate tangerines.
The warm spot is too hot, so I can't sit there.
The children gathered on the warm part of the floor.
I tucked the rice bowl under the blanket on the warm spot of the floor.

explain: 온돌방에서 불을 때는 곳과 가까워 바닥이 가장 따뜻한 쪽이에요. 반대말은 '윗목'이에요. 겨울에 가족이 이불 속에 발을 넣고 모이던 장면과 함께 자주 나와요.
explain_en: In an ondol room, it is the part of the floor closest to the heat source and warmest. Its opposite is '윗목'. It often appears in scenes of family gathering with their feet under a blanket in winter.

examples.ko: 어림으로 계산해도 대략 만 원쯤 나와요.
examples.en: Even by rough calculation it comes to about ten thousand won.

examples.ko: 제 어림에는 그 일이 한 시간이면 끝날 것 같아요.
examples.en: By my estimate, that job will be done in an hour.
Roughly a hundred people came.

examples.ko: 눈으로 어림을 해 보니 길이가 두 미터쯤 돼요.
examples.en: Eyeballing it, the length is about two meters.

examples.ko: 시험 점수를 어림해 보면 팔십 점 정도예요.
examples.en: If I estimate my test score, it is around eighty.
I walked on a rough guess and got lost.

explain: 어림은 정확하게 재지 않고 대충 짐작하는 것이라서 '어림잡다', '어림짐작'처럼 다른 말과 붙어서 자주 나와요. '대충'은 일을 성의 없이 할 때도 쓰지만, 어림은 수나 양을 짐작할 때 주로 써요.

phrases.en: You want to buy it at this price? No way.
phrases.nuance_ko: 상대의 부탁이나 기대를 강하게 거절할 때 써요. 말투가 세서 친한 사이에서 주로 말해요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used to firmly turn down someone's request or expectation. It sounds strong, so it is mostly said between people who are close.

explain_en: 어림 is rough guessing without measuring exactly, so it usually appears inside words like '어림잡다' and '어림짐작'. '대충' can also mean doing a job carelessly, but 어림 is mainly for guessing numbers or amounts.

examples.ko: 많이 걸었으니 요쯤에서 잠깐 쉬어 가요.
examples.en: We've walked a lot, so let's rest a bit around here.

examples.ko: 요쯤이면 거의 다 온 것 같아요.
examples.en: I think we're almost there by around here.

examples.ko: 오늘 일은 요쯤 해 두고 나머지는 내일 해요.
examples.en: Let's stop around this point today and do the rest tomorrow.

examples.ko: 제 지갑을 요쯤에 두었는데 안 보여요.
examples.en: I put my wallet around here, but I can't see it.
I'll finish today's class at about this point.

examples.ko: 어릴 때는 키가 요쯤 오던 아이가 벌써 저보다 커요.
examples.en: The child who used to be only about this tall is already taller than I am.

explain: '이쯤'의 작은말로, 장소·정도·시점을 가볍게 짚을 때 써요. '요쯤에서 그만하자'처럼 어디까지 하고 멈출지 정할 때 자주 나와요. 같은 뜻의 '여기쯤'도 많이 써요.
explain_en: It is the small form of '이쯤', lightly pinpointing a place, degree or moment. It often appears when deciding where to stop, as in '요쯤에서 그만하자'. '여기쯤' is a common equivalent.

examples.ko: 피아노로 도레미파솔라시도 음계를 천천히 쳐 보세요.
examples.en: Try playing the do-re-mi scale slowly on the piano.

examples.ko: 이 곡은 음계가 단순해서 어린이도 쉽게 따라 불러요.
examples.en: This song has a simple scale, so even children can sing along easily.
I start every morning with scale practice.

examples.ko: 음계를 외우면 악보 읽기가 훨씬 쉬워져요.
examples.en: If you memorize the scales, reading sheet music gets much easier.

examples.ko: 동양 음악은 서양과 다른 음계를 써요.
examples.en: Eastern music uses scales different from Western music.

examples.ko: 음계에 맞게 노래를 부르는 연습을 했어요.
examples.en: We practiced singing in tune with the scale.

explain: 음악 시간에 자주 나오는 말이고 '장음계'(밝은 느낌), '단음계'(어두운 느낌)로 나눠요. '음정'은 두 소리 사이의 높이 차이를 말해서 '음계'와 달라요. '음계 연습'은 악기를 배울 때 기본이에요.
explain_en: It comes up often in music class and is divided into '장음계' (bright feel) and '단음계' (dark feel). '음정' is the pitch gap between two sounds, so it differs from '음계'. '음계 연습' is a basic part of learning an instrument.

examples.en: The straight-line distance from my house to school is about one kilometer.
It's close in a straight line, but far by road.
What is the straight-line distance between the two cities?
I measured the straight-line distance on the map.
To go in a straight line, you have to cross the mountain.

examples.ko: 서울과 부산의 직선거리는 삼백 킬로미터가 넘어요.
examples.en: The straight-line distance between Seoul and Busan is over three hundred kilometers.

explain: 길을 따라 실제로 가는 거리가 아니라 두 곳을 곧게 이은 거리예요. 그래서 '직선거리로는 가깝다'처럼 실제 이동 거리와 비교할 때 많이 말해요. 실제 이동 거리는 보통 '도로 거리'나 '걸리는 시간'으로 말해요.
explain_en: It is the distance of a straight line between two points, not the distance you actually travel along roads. That is why people say things like '직선거리로는 가깝다' to compare it with the real trip. The actual travel distance is usually described as '도로 거리' or by travel time.

en: to interrogate; to question thoroughly; to press hard

examples.en: Reporters pressed the minister about responsibility for the incident.

examples.ko: 친구가 왜 거짓말을 했냐고 계속 추궁해요.
examples.en: My friend keeps pressing me about why I lied.

examples.ko: 너무 몰아붙이며 추궁하면 사실을 말하기 어려워요.
examples.en: If you press someone too hard, it's difficult for them to tell the truth.

examples.ko: 국회에서 의원들이 예산 낭비 문제를 추궁하고 있어요.
examples.en: In the National Assembly, lawmakers are grilling officials about the wasted budget.

examples.ko: 잘못을 추궁하기보다 해결 방법을 먼저 찾아요.
examples.en: Instead of pressing for who is at fault, let's find a solution first.

examples.ko: 선생님이 지각한 이유를 추궁하지 않고 그냥 넘어가 주셨어요.
examples.en: My teacher didn't press me about why I was late and just let it go.

explain: '따지다'나 '캐묻다'와 비슷하지만 잘못이나 책임을 끝까지 파고들 때 써요. '책임을 추궁하다', '이유를 추궁하다'처럼 쓰고, '~에게 ~을 추궁하다' 구조도 많아요. 일상에서는 '따지다'가 더 편하게 들려요.
explain_en: It is similar to '따지다' or '캐묻다' but is used when you keep digging into someone's fault or responsibility. It appears as '책임을 추궁하다' or '이유를 추궁하다', and also in the pattern '~에게 ~을 추궁하다'. In casual speech, '따지다' sounds more relaxed.

examples.en: The prices at this shop are absurdly high.

examples.ko: 터무니없이 높은 집값 때문에 이사를 포기했어요.
examples.en: I gave up on moving because of the unreasonably high housing prices.
The time to prepare for the exam was ridiculously short.

examples.ko: 동생이 터무니없이 많은 간식을 사 왔어요.
examples.en: My younger sibling brought home an absurd amount of snacks.

examples.ko: 터무니없이 달게 만든 케이크를 한 입 먹고 물을 마셨어요.
examples.en: I took one bite of the ridiculously sweet cake and drank some water.

examples.ko: 오늘은 사람이 터무니없이 많아서 줄이 끝이 없어요.
examples.en: There are so many people today that the line never ends.

explain: 뒤에 '비싸다, 부족하다, 많다'처럼 정도를 나타내는 말이 자주 와서 '상식에 안 맞을 만큼'이라는 느낌을 줘요. 형용사 '터무니없다'는 '터무니없는 소리/생각'처럼 명사 앞에서 써요. 일상에서는 '말도 안 되게'라고도 해요.
explain_en: It often comes before words of degree like '비싸다, 부족하다, 많다' and gives a feel of 'beyond all common sense'. The adjective form '터무니없다' is used before nouns, as in '터무니없는 소리/생각'. In daily talk people also say '말도 안 되게'.

en: to climb down a mountain; to go down a mountain

examples.en: We came down right after lunch.
It is better to come down before it gets dark.

examples.ko: 날씨가 나빠져서 정상까지 못 가고 하산했어요.
examples.en: The weather got bad, so we went down without reaching the top.

examples.ko: 다른 길로 하산하면 다른 마을이 나와요.
examples.en: If you go down another trail, you reach a different village.

examples.ko: 천천히 하산할 때는 지팡이가 도움이 돼요.
examples.en: A walking stick helps when you descend slowly.
After coming down, I ate warm gukbap.

explain: 등산 이야기에서 '내려오다' 대신 써서 산에서 내려오는 뜻이 분명해져요. '정상에서 하산하다', '다른 길로 하산하다'처럼 써요. 산이 아닌 곳에는 안 써요.
explain_en: In hiking talk it replaces '내려오다' and makes clear you are descending a mountain. Use it like '정상에서 하산하다' or '다른 길로 하산하다'. It isn't used for places other than mountains.
